utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As you know, we were scheduled to commence at 8.00 a.m. We are late because we were informed that the accused Milan Lukic is unwell. We were waiting to see whether he would arrive. He has not arrived. Our understanding is that he will come later. His illness is not of the kind that would prevent him attending, but we can't deal with any substantive matters in his absence, because I understand he does wish to be present. Mr. Alarid, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That is my understanding, Your Honour. My case manager spoke with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I apologise, I forget the microphone. Your Honour, my case manager spoke with Mr. Lukic about 7.38, and he indicated that he was not well. He did indicate that he wanted to be present for these witnesses especially in light of some of the identification issues that came into play and especially since, apparently, especially the second witness does identify Mr. Lukic, although in a belated manner in the statements, but I think it is imperative that per his request he be present for these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll -- we'll wait, but in the meantime I have some administrative matters to deal with, and I'll take the opportunity to deal with them, and I'll also give a decision on Prosecution motion under Rule 92 ter. Today, as you know, we'll stop at 12.00. That is to enable the Judges to attend a very important meeting of the Plenary. I have reorganised the sitting hours, the sitting schedule slightly. We will begin in the mornings at 8.50, ten minutes to 9.00. If my arithmetic is bad then you must correct me. It means, then, that we would go from 8.50 to 10.20. We will take a 20-minute break to 10.40. The next session will be 10.40 to 12.10. We would then take a half an hour break, 12.10 to 12.40, and we would then sit from 12.40 to 1.45. If this presents any logistical problems for the registry or the detention unit, then I should be advised as quickly as possible. I will take the opportunity to give a decision on the Prosecution motion in respect of those witnesses who are to testify this week. There are five witnesses which are the subject of Prosecution's motion under Rule 92 ter, filed on the 15th of February, 2008, and a supplemental motion filed on the 8th of August. By the motion of the 8th of August, the Prosecution sought to supplement with seven witness statements, and three of those statements relate to witnesses who are scheduled to testify this week. It also requested permission to assign 65 ter numbers to certain material, the subject of the motion of the 15th of February, as well as the seven statements. The Defence of Sredoje Lukic responded on the 28th of February, and the Defence of Milan Lukic responded on the 28th March. Neither party responded to the motion of the 8th of August. The Chamber has reviewed the evidence submitted in the two motions with regard to the five witnesses under consideration, and its conclusion is that the transcripts, the statements, and the associated exhibits are admissible under Rule 92 ter provided the requirements of that Rule are met. The Chamber will also grant the motion of the 8th of August insofar as it requests permission to assign Rule 65 ter numbers. And of course the Chamber will remain seized of the two motions insofar as the remaining witnesses are concerned. And I bring to your attention the fact that the Chamber issued a decision last Friday concerning Mevsud Poljo, who is a Rule 92 bis witness and is to be called for cross-examination this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn for half an hour. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, just to use this opportunity to raise some -- some issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave, please. Thank you. Firstly, we received this morning supplemental information sheet from OTP at 7.20, so I kindly ask my learned friend for OTP if we can receive a little bit earlier those kind of informations to have enough time to be prepared for examination. That is the first issue. And second issue also related to witness notification. On first day we received witness notification at 6.20 p.m. So I kindly ask my learned friends if it is possible before 4.00 p.m. on Thursday to receive the witness notification for the next week. And third issue is related to my client. We would like to use opportunity according to European Convention of Human Rights Article 6.3D and according to the practice from the Prlic case, my client would like to ask -- potentially to ask just a very few questions of very few witnesses. Of course the questions for those witnesses my learned friend Mr. Dieckmann and I will lead but just to use this opportunity with your leave, if the Trial Chamber grants that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In my view you need to file a motion for something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would need to have it properly considered. File a motion setting out your submission and any authority on which you rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, may I ask the Prosecutor why the information that should have been issued by Thursday of last week was only transmitted to the Defence this morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If you're talking about the witness notification that was issued on Thursday at 6.20. I believe that's what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Last Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's in the evening. 6.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll try to get it in before the close of business --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the information that was transmitted this morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I believe he might be talking about an addendum to one of the witness's statements. When I proofed the witness this weekend he asked to make some changes to his statement and we drafted up an addendum and had it translated and everything yesterday and we did send it to counsel by e-mail last evening but we did it -- we transmitted it as soon as it was finished. So we have -- this is -- this is a factor that comes up in proofing. Rather than submit proofing notes, which is the custom, the witness felt that he wanted to make certain changes, and we felt it better to do an addendum to his statement rather than me drafting proofing notes and submitting the changes myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I guess -- so you proofed the witness over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question might then be asked why was the witness only proofed over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, that's the standard practice in the Tribunal, Your Honour. We can't go down to -- to the region to proof all of our witnesses although we'd prefer to do that. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. May I make a correction? Since Defence counsel is not real clear when he said he received -- he did receive something this morning which was in relation to Mr. Ossogo's witness, but I don't -- I believe that they were proofing notes as well, and this witness was also proofed yesterday. So Defence counsel did receive the addendum to the statement of my witness last evening, but received the proofing notes for the other witness this morning. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Every effort should be made to have the statements that are to be transmitted on Thursday transmitted by, I would say, 4.00, 4.00 p.m. 6.20 p.m. is a little late. The order that the Chamber made didn't deal with a specific time, but I would say now that we ought to be working for 4.00 p.m. as a deadline.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will abide by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And that of course will also apply to the Defence when their time comes. We are going to adjourn for half an hour and see whether the accused arrives, but I believe now there is some information from the court deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm now told by the court deputy that he is scheduled to arrive at 10 minutes to 9.00. So we will resume at 10 minutes to 9.00. We are adjourned. --- Break taken at 8.19 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I see you're here. You are here, and you're fit? Not hearing. I was saying we were sorry to learn that you were indisposed, but we're happy to see you here now. THE ACCUSED M. LUKIC: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the interpretation for Mr. Lukic's response? THE ACCUSED M. LUKIC: [Interpretation] I was given some pills to take, Your Honour, but I do still have a stomach ache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We note that you're here, and we hope that you'll be well enough to -- to follow the proceedings. Mr. Prosecutor, will you call your first -- THE ACCUSED M. LUKIC: [Interpretation] Well, I said I wasn't feeling well. I'm still not feeling well. I was given some medication, but I'm not still feeling well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that impact in any way on your ability to follow the morning's proceedings? THE ACCUSED M. LUKIC: [Interpretation] Yes, it does impact my ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, in speaking with Mr. Lukic ever so briefly, and actually my case manager doing that, he indicated that although he took pills this morning for his condition he's afraid that, one, that it's bothering him now and that it may necessitate him in sort of an emergency scenario to leave the courtroom at any time and that is the problem that could both disrupt the proceedings and impact his ability, I think, to pay attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you making a specific submission, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the situation I think it would be disruptive if Mr. Lukic was having to leave to use the restroom or whatnot and I don't know if it would be possible to postpone the proceedings of this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid and Mr. Lukic, what the Chamber has decided is that we will start the proceedings, but if Mr. Lukic finds it necessary to -- to leave for the bathroom, then he should let us know, and of course we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please call the first witness. Mr. Ossogo, is it your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This will be the third Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Prosecution is calling Witness VG-022. I would like to give the court officer the pseudonym sheet so that it can be given to the witness and so he can recognise his name, and this sheet should be shown to the Chamber and to Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-22, on the sheet that you have in front of you, do you see the letters VG-022 and the name next -- and the name next to this pseudonym, is it your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: The bottom of the sheet, you will find two other names, names that you may refer to during your testimony. Do you recognise these two names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the sheet to the Trial Chamber now. And once the documents will have been shown to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence, the Prosecution would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, I notice that you have two pseudonyms on that sheet. In fact -- in fact, three. I think it would be more convenient to have one pseudonym for each sheet so that there's no confusion, but we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit P13 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your comment, and we will take this into account, Your Honour. This is why we had written the witness's pseudonym in very large font, whereas the two other witnesses that he may refer to were in smaller font. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-22, you have been granted protective measures for your safety. The Trial Chamber granted these protective measures. You will benefit from face and voice distortion, but please during your testimony could you refrain from giving any indications as to your address or as to the name of your relatives, but in case this happens I will remind you of this. Now, we -- we have information in one of your previous statements on what you were doing at the time. What are you doing now, Witness VG-22? What's your occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I am the director of a private firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you lived in 1992, in early 1992? But don't tell us the address. Just give us the municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I lived and resided in Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do give us the month -- the month in 1992 when you lived there, and did you live there throughout 1992 or only for part of that year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: In Visegrad I lived until May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you have children at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to the testimony you made in this Tribunal in the Vasiljevic case in September 10th, 2001. Have you read the -- were you already heard in this Tribunal on September 10, 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I do not think that I gave any statements before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I would like to know whether you testified in the Vasiljevic case, Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, I did take the stand in the Vasiljevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: September 10th, 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague this weekend, were you able to read your -- the transcript of your testimony in this case, in the Mitar Vasiljevic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: To your knowledge, this transcript you listened to, was it faithful to what you actually said when you were in court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution would like now to tender the following exhibit: The transcript of the hearing in this court of Witness VG-022 on September 10, 2001. This is 65 ter document 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit P14, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-22, the Defence and the Trial Chamber have the transcript of your testimony in the Mitar case -- in the Vasiljevic case, and this document has been tendered as evidence, so we'll not go back to everything you said at the time, but I just would like to ask you some additional questions to get some details. I would like to ask you a few questions on the White Eagles, the paramilitary formation called the White Eagles. Do you know this formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there existed such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In which year and where did this formation exist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, already in 1992 that unit was set up, and it operated in part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as far as I know, in particular in its eastern part, namely, Visegrad and the surroundings of the town of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you have any information on the strength of this unit in this region where they operated, the strength of the White Eagles in the Visegrad region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I could not say what their number was with precision, but these units were not of the type of conventional army units, a thousand soldiers strong or something like that. They were smaller units in number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You say the White Eagles were operating. Could you tell us what it means?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Ossogo. The interpreter wants the witness to come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I'll come back to -- so I'll repeat my question. You said that they operated in Visegrad, that the White Eagles operated in that area. What exactly did you mean when you said they operated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, one could say that these paramilitary formations had been set up illegally, and they worked and acted in contravention of the regulations and laws that were in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and for the most part they did harmful -- they undertook harmful actions or impermissible actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can you be a bit more specific when you say that they undertook harmful actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, I can. For the most part in their activity they would intimidate people, expel people, and they would commit murders of the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say non-Serbs, which group are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: For the most part in the municipality of Visegrad, apart from the Serb population the majority consisted of Bosniaks, of Muslims. So this primarily refers to that population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: The White Eagles were undertaking illegal activities against Muslims, is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether there was any connection between the White Eagles and the JNA, which at the time was in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. There did exist such a connection, and evidence of that is the fact that the very commander of the Yugoslav People's Army, the commander of the town said so on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you give the Trial Chamber the name of this JNA commander you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The commander of the town at the time self-styled, self-designated, self-appointed commander of the town was a man by the name of Jovanovic, and he was a lieutenant colonel by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic, did he say anything at one point in time that would be related to the White Eagles, maybe during a meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He explicitly and clearly, in front of 4.000 people, and I myself was present, stated that the White Eagles units were present in Visegrad and that they were under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When he indicated that the White Eagles were under his command, did he mean that the White Eagles were under the integrated command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Leading.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. That's leading. You're telling the witness the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-22, could you tell us what Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic said when he referred to the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. At the time he clearly said at the football stadium where there were, in my estimation, at least 4.000 Muslims present, he said, "The units of the White Eagles are also under my command, so mind your behaviour and watch your steps, because," and then the -- "or else, or else," and everybody was present knew exactly what that "or else" meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You said that -- that people -- there were about 4.000 people in front of Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic when he addressed them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: They were exclusively Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: They were all inhabitants of Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Why did they get together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The people assembled there because the danger was threatening them of liquidation. This is what they thought. And they were in smaller groups, and then escorted and organised by the Yugoslav People's Army they assembled at the football stadium there in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was -- who was threatening them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: There were no verbal threats of the kind directly uttered then, but it was quite clear to everybody that lieutenant colonel was actually saying that he meant to say that the units were under his command and that if he so wanted they would be active or not be active, and if they were active one knew what that meant. That meant merciless liquidation of all Muslims that they came across.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And the people who got together, these 4.000 people, were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. They were solely civilians, exclusively civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that the Yugoslav People's Army leave Visegrad and the White Eagles, did they stay in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. After the departure of the Yugoslav People's Army, those units remained on in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: These units remaining in Visegrad, did they continue operating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, they did. To my knowledge, they continued to operate intensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-22, I'm now going to talk about your departure from Visegrad, because at the beginning of your testimony you said that you stayed in Visegrad up to the month of May 1992. Did you leave Visegrad in the year -- in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: With my entire family I went in the direction of Serbia, directly to the town of Uzice and farther beyond that to Pristina and some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I left Visegrad because I was afraid for my life and the lives of my family members. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you left Visegrad, using what kind of transportation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I left Visegrad with my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Have you been helped by anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: By whom? By whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: When I was leaving Visegrad I was given direct help by Mr. Stanko Pecikoza, who was the vice-president of the Serbian Democratic Party, and he was an influential man in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you personally know Mr. Stanko Pecikoza apart from the professional connections you had with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I knew him well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Based on what I know, Mr. Stanko Pecikoza was liquidated by the White Eagle units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When you say "liquidated," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I mean that they carried out this murder. They killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: As far as you know, do you have any information about the people who murdered him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Based on what I know, Your Honours, they were members of these paramilitary formations. And there were also stories. There was talk that it was a certain gentleman by the name of Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: If it is possible, can you tell us whom you heard this information from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I received this information from several sources, and among other sources also from the family members of Stanko Pecikoza who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: If it is possible, could you give us more details, details concerning the family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how much of an effect that would have on the security or safety of the people who gave me this information. No problem. I can tell you more details once this is taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, do you have an application to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We can continue and maybe start a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ossogo, you have completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, in the time I had been allocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. VG-22, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, at the time that the war broke out -- [French interpretation on English channel].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is this a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes. Or it's a statement. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, you could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You were a head of your party under the new two-party system?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me bring it to your attention that the question which you asked did not come out in the English interpretation, so please ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you were a leader of your party under the new two-party system in place in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I was not a president of the party. I was one of the vice-presidents. And if I can just add, this was not a two-party system. It was a multi-party system that was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, but isn't it true that basically two parties were in control, the SDA and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: That is correct. They had the majority in the Assembly. Those two parties had an absolute majority in the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the SDA was primarily a Muslim party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The majority of its members were Muslims, Muslim Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And because of the demographics of the area, the majority of the Assembly was SDA as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. At these elections the SDA, the Democratic Action Party, did win the majority of the votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how long had you been part of this Assembly before the fighting started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not a member of the Municipal Assembly of Visegrad. At that time, I was in the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I apologise, sir. I read in your initial statement that you were a Member of Parliament, and so I assumed you were an elected official before that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The first time I was elected to the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in 1990, and I was in that body until the new elections in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what happened to your position in parliament while the war was being fought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Nothing special happened. When I was able to, I attended the sessions, and if I was prevented from attending because of the war, then I didn't attend, and then nothing particular happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the parliament was not doing any real business while the fighting was occurring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: If you're thinking of the Assembly of the Visegrad municipality, it worked with difficulty. And also the same thing applies for the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It also worked with difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, would it be fair to say that it did not work at all due to the fact that it was actually the Serbians and the army that had taken control of the countryside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: This was a short period, from the time the conflict broke out until the time that the Yugoslav People's Army took over power in the town. But this didn't -- it wasn't a long period of time, perhaps 20 days at the most. And when we're talking about the work of the parliament, this is a relatively short period in that sense, so you cannot really say that it was or wasn't functioning during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, then maybe a better question to ask is who had power over Visegrad in April/May of 1992? Real power.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: In that period, the army -- or, rather, the Yugoslav People's Army had the real power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who controlled the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The main command of the -- or the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav People's Army was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, would you please speculate as to when you believe the plans of Belgrade were made to take over Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: This is very hard to say, Your Honours. I really cannot. I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me kind of give you a couple points of reference. At what point in time were the Muslim population disarmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The question is not precise, so it's kind of hard. Muslim Bosniaks were not in some separate organised units where they were armed. There was the Territorial Defence, which was an organ of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all were members of that body, all those who lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you're thinking about the disarming of the Territorial Defence, then you could describe it in this way. It happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please do that. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. From what I can recall, this happened about three or four months before the intense conflict began.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the intense conflict being about the 4th or 5th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: You could take that date as a marker point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who disarmed the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was disarmed by the army. Pursuant to orders of the JNA, all the weapons in the possession of the Territorial Defence were withdrawn. They were taken by them and probably placed in different barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this is the same JNA that was controlled by Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so even though the entire JNA army didn't come in until later, there were troops in the region organising the disarmament?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: When you say the Yugoslav People's Army, this is the army that had its barracks throughout Yugoslav army, and this means Bosnia and Herzegovina also, and there were such barracks -- or two such barracks in the territory of the municipality of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that just by the demographics and population that the majority of the Territorial Defence was Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: As you said it yourself, in view of the demographics probably the composition of the Territorial Defence reflected that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so practically speaking, the disarmament had the effect of leaving the Muslims without ordinary weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: You could say that, although the Territorial Defence, I repeat, was not an ethnic unit. These were constitutionally and legally regulated reserve units. And in case of need, they were the ones which could react quickly in a specific territory to protect the law and so on and so forth. That's why they were called the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with the breakdown of order then, still the ordinary Territorial Defence would be unable to protect the laws of that territory. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: You could say that, although I would not agree with you when you say when the order broke down. Everything functioned, although with difficulty, until the Yugoslav People's Army came.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And there's been evidence that the people's -- Yugoslav People's Army came in under the pretense that Muslims were killing people, slaughtering Serbians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: You could hear such reports on the radio broadcast by some radio stations from Serbia, specifically Radio Titovo Uzice broadcast such news items.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How did it make you feel being a local that knew the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, sir, a person could not feel at ease. It's a very uncomfortable feeling. You think they are not well informed over there, and you try through friends, by telephone and so on to explain to the radio station that things are not the way they see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with the disarmament of the Territorial Defence, at best a few people had small arms but no heavy weapons or artillery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you first heard the heavy artillery and mortars being used because you knew that the Territorial Defence had been disarmed, would it be fair to say that that was the Yugoslav army using the artillery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: When they began to act or fire around town using the mortars and shells, it was not possible to know exactly what was happening, but the assumption was that these were paramilitary formations organised or acting with the approval of the Serbian Democratic Party. I had, for example, such --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you at the translation. Do you want to continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, I more or less completed my answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the Serbian Democratic Party was the minority party in Visegrad; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't that insignificant, but the SDA party had more votes and then right behind that party was the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But with the Muslim population being under attack, didn't that practically put the Serbian Democratic Party in power?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Not just because of that, but later when the JNA came they installed these people from the SDA to positions of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you explain why the JNA didn't put people of your party in power considering that you were lawfully elected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that was because the Yugoslav People's Army was not what it was before. It was called the Yugoslav People's Army just the same, but actually it was the army of Serbia comprising exclusively Serb personnel, and that was the main reason why they did that. They expelled legally elected representatives and appointed mostly people from the Serbian Democratic Party in their place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so would it be fair to say that this is evidence of a prior plan by those who controlled the JNA to replace the Muslims in power in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I cannot assert that that can be considered evidence, but it's not far from the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who were these people that were in power after the JNA left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I wasn't in Visegrad at that time, but later from conversations I know that they were people of Serb ethnicity exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, for instance, before the -- the shooting started, the police force was a joint force of both Muslims and Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And of that, the -- who was the commander of the police before the break-apart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I really couldn't give you the exact name. I can't remember right at this time who the police commander was. As for the chief of police who by hierarchy has the highest rank and is the most senior person was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name. The witness perhaps could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please repeat the name of the chief.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Seval Murtic was the chief of the Visegrad police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who replaced him after the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Immediately upon the arrival of the Yugoslav People's Army, not long after that the chief of the police was Professor Risto, and the police commander was Dragan Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so the head was Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And second in command was Tomic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what was the authority of -- of these two positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Their powers were precisely spelled out by law. They were the standard powers that such persons, persons in such positions, such officials, have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And these were -- and this was power to command all of the police and supposed to protect the laws of all citizens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In your opinion, did these two commanders protect the citizens of Visegrad, including Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Judging by later developments, they did not discharge their functions the way they should have discharged it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were they put in place by the Yugoslav commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, I think that they installed them in those posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And by hierarchy would that mean that their command would come really from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The people who appointed Mr. Tomic and the chief, the head, those people had their superiors and their command in Belgrade, and that's for certain. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Crisis Staff after the Uzice Corps left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The commander of the Crisis Staff or the president of the Assembly upon the departure of the Yugoslav People's Army from Visegrad was Branimir Savovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he was also appointed from Belgrade or took his orders from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I do not think that there was a direct chain of ordering or a command, because Branimir Savovic was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party for Visegrad municipality, and it was probably on that basis that he was the president of the Assembly and ipso facto the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you believe he took orders from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I personally do not think that he received orders from Belgrade. His orders came from the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, Radovan Karadzic, and the seat of the -- that party was at Pale, a town near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, with regards to -- would it be fair to say that Serbs that did not cooperate with this new power structure were at risk?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that there was a pattern of forced conscription into the service of the army for Serbians in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, one could say that it was the way you described it, except that the word "forced" could be more adequately replaced by the expression "regular call-ups," because under the law then everybody had to respond to such call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But under the law of the time, that everybody would have included Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But Muslims were not being called up. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And during the time that the army was in Visegrad, there was still lootings and burnings and damage to Muslims' property, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Muslims were being removed from their homes and some of them were disappearing or liquidated; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Things like that happened, and they happened that way, but perhaps one should emphasise that this was a relatively small number of cases if we take into consideration the situation which actually obtained at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But it was not stopped during this time that the Yugoslav army was in town; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but, Your Honours, by your leave if I can add this: To my knowledge and as far as I could see, the Yugoslav People's Army opposed and countered this, and they eliminated -- rather, prevented such cases. And if such cases were reported to them, they would intervene, so that eventually it became a less frequent practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: This was just for a few weeks, this appearance of less frequent practice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, so far you've used half an hour for your cross-examination, and I'll give you another half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say nothing obliges you to use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that these less frequent cases were during a short period of time of the army's full presence in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, one could say that. In view of the fact that such incidents, if one could call it an incident if you expel a person from his own house or torch his house, happened every day or every second day, and then you wouldn't have such cases for three or four days because the Yugoslav People's Army had taken action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did they take action, or maybe it was just the appearance of action.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I couldn't say with precision. It could be either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You attended the 4.000-person meeting at the stadium; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: At that meeting you had found your own family who you had lost contact with for a few days; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So this was a time of great terror and uncertainty for you to know that your family was not safe or not have any good word of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at this football stadium there's this Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he wasn't a friend of the Muslims in that stadium that night, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: You could put it that way, but he acted in his professional capacity as a professional soldier, as an officer. I did not gain the impression that he personally, as a person, had anything against the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: He threatened the crowd with the White Eagles. He claimed that they were under his control.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is that the words of a friend of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, I think that that was a method whereby he wanted to preserve firm control in town and avoid his men having any problems or him having any problems and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid. Perhaps you have dealt with that point sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just got word from my case manager that Mr. Lukic is not feeling well right now, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you what. I think we'll just take the half an hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: VG-22, after the army left, the SDS took control; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Savovic was the leader of the SDS at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, early on in this process you dealt with Savovic as a leader; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this began following the capture of 12 Serbian -- Bosnian Serbians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. By leave, Your Honours, I should just like to -- to say that I knew Savovic not only from that moment, but I had known him before and we had dealings even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But the point I'm trying to make is that you dealt with him as the leader of the situation at the time that you're dealing also with the 12 Serbian prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell the Court about the capture of the 12 Serbians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: In brief, police patrols, and in fact the Territorial Defence units that were already functional at that time were tasked with inspecting the territory, touring the territory where problems were cropping up or were expected to crop up. So in such -- one of such inspection tours they ran into 12 armed men who belonged to neither any police or Territorial Defence unit. As these men were armed, as such they were arrested and brought into the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: From -- do you recall giving a statement in this case long before your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this was a statement given back in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Just -- it is possible that that is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, on -- in that statement you indicated that the captured Serbs were locals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, they were all locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And they were in camouflage and police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Then why were they taken prisoner if -- because they were part of a police unit, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: No. You see, they did have police uniforms on, but they were not part of the hierarchy. They were not members, not official members of the police force but of some -- I don't know. They represented a different group, some other group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you got to meet them; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you even got them -- to know them a little bit since you released them; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Your Honours, can I just say this? It was not me, myself, personally who set them free. It was a decision of the organs of municipal authority which I just executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you were dealing personally with Savovic regarding their release; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you wanted to exchange them for Muslim women and children; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: No, that is not the way it was. There had been some proposals. Savovic's deputies or assistants put forward some proposals, but they themselves did not believe that to be a viable, a realistic option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because they demanded the unconditional release of these 12 soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: At the negotiations in question, they did insist on an unconditional surrender of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So they were not disavowed as criminals, but they were embraced as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: They were not considered to be criminals, but it was known that they were a group of armed men who most probably were under the control and command of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that was acknowledged by Savovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: We did not talk about it directly, because that could be sensed in a way. It was implied that that was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But in fact you knew that one of the members of the 12 was the assistant to the commander of the police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Wouldn't the assistant to the commander be considered a person of responsibility in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, he did discharge that function, but he wilfully abandoned that post and transferred himself into an informal armed group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How do you know he wilfully abandoned that post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I know that because I was in practically daily contact with representatives of the organs in power, representatives of the police, and I even personally talked to him directly at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: After the JNA left, were there check-points with policemen manning them in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: After the JNA had left, well, I couldn't say with precision because I wasn't there in that period, but I suppose that there were such check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that Muslims needed proper paperwork to come and go freely from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who had the authority to give that paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Until the arrival of the army no one needed any such documents. Once the army took over command in the municipality and town, initially they were the ones who issued the permits for movement, and later on it was the police station that did so. And let me add for a period it was also the so-called National Defence or the Territorial Defence. They were over a period vested with the power of issuing such passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who at the police station issued such passes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, passes were issued by the chief of the police at the time, Risto Perisic, and also the commander of the police, Dragan Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that vehicles were being taken away by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, there had been such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And including a vehicle of yours that was owned by the company you worked for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. The police confiscated that vehicle with the explanation that they needed it and gave the explanation that when they had the number of vehicles that they required they would return that vehicle to the owner or to the company that they took it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did they give you paperwork proving that the car was taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically, but I think as far as I can recall I didn't get any kind of paper of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone got proper paperwork?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps they did, perhaps they didn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you hear of many such confiscations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: As far as I know, it wasn't really something that happened on a large scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many Muslim villages were left at the Visegrad territory during the Crisis Staff governing period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: You mean what was the size of the population, or are you asking me how many villages there were?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm asking how many villages were left afterwards or in existence, and if you wanted to talk about the population, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: From what I understand of the question, the answer would be some villages that were in the immediate vicinity of the town, some kilometre or two away, these houses remained. All the other houses that were farther away from town were burned or knocked down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I may have asked you this already, but who was governing Visegrad after the JNA left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: After the JNA left. Well, when they were still there the army formed the organs of power, the Assembly, which they -- to which they appointed mostly members of the SDS, and then the executive organs, too, were the same, the police. All these organs were also installed by the Yugoslav People's Army, and this was all 100 per cent personnel of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so it was based on this trickle down of appointments that the Crisis Staff or the SDS installed the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that Muslims were having to pay to get a permit to leave the city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: According to what I know, these were rare cases. That wasn't the rule, pay and then you will be able to leave town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In those cases, to whom were they paying the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I don't know of such a large number of these cases, but it was up to each person to do the best they could if they could find a connection or something, but there was no rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Wouldn't that connection have to be to the top of the police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I really couldn't say how these people managed to do this, to get out of town. And if they had any contacts with the police leadership, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, of the 12 -- in your statement, you indicated that of the 12 people captured or Serbians captured, one of them was of the last name Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your statement it indicates that you did not know the first name. Do you know the first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Probably at that time I couldn't recall it. Now I think that I do know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what do you think you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I think that it was Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not the timekeeper, but I have a sense that you're very near to the end. Six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What were the names of the members of the Crisis Staff headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you all the names. I can just assume that the Crisis Staff formed by the SDS later comprised the people who later took up these positions, the president of the municipality, the police commander, the chief of police, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what was the date that these 12 gentlemen were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I really cannot remember the exact date, but it could have been perhaps the 15th of April, approximately, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was the date of the assembly in the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: The assembly at the football stadium was on the same day that the army, the Yugoslav People's Army, took total control over the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- in relation to the 15th of April, was that before or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: These people were captured before the Yugoslav People's Army took control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that the stories regarding Milan Lukic are all hearsay, secondhand, or even third-hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. It's a very general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't agree with you, Mr. Ossogo. I think it is within the -- this witness's competence to say whether on the basis of what he knows what has been said about the accused is based on information gathered from other people or even secondhand hearsay as was put to him by counsel. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as Milan -- Mr. Milan Lukic is concerned, I did not know him. I'm seeing him for the first time. And from what I know about his activities, my personal knowledge -- I don't have any personal experience or any personal contacts. All I know are things that come from talk of friends, acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could only one microphone be on at a time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And of the witnesses or these people that you heard stories from, would it be fair to say that they have -- it may have even been stories from other people that they were relaying to you in a third-hand way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, you know how things go. If things are happening like the things that were happening in Visegrad, then these things are told first-hand, secondhand, third-hand. There was a lot of talk about these things. So you have different information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that as stories pass through many people, the details can change or be exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure he can help you with that. He can't help you with that, Mr. Alarid. You can address us on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Fair enough, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that other than those secondhand stories, you have no personal knowledge of Mr. Milan Lukic being a commander of anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I personally do not. Like I said before, I didn't have any direct or indirect contacts with the gentleman, and I don't have any personal or specific contacts or any information that could come from personal contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Are you aware he was a local citizen of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone knows that. Actually, excuse me, from what I know he was born in Visegrad and lived there for a certain period of time. After that he lived and worked in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this you've learned from stories; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't call them stories. These were conversations with people who knew him well, who went to school with him, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- and if we have to move to private session, can you tell me who those people are?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Witness VG-22, a very good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, VG-22. My name is Jens Dieckmann and I am Defence co-counsel for Mr. Sredoje Lukic. I just have several questions. If you cannot understand me, please just indicate it immediately so then I can repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: VG-22, as we have already learned, you have given, on the one hand, an interview, a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecution in 1997/1998. It's true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This interview, you have had the opportunity to give all information you have been aware and of -- you know correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And as far as you remember, you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I think that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you have been aware that with your signature you declare that these statements are truth -- the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Very fine. And on 10 September 2001, you have given testimony in the Vasiljevic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And again -- sorry. And again, in this testimony you have already had the opportunity to give all names and all informations you have been aware of; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Now, you have given your testimony under oath declaring that this is the truth and nothing but the truth. You remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Very well. First of all, before I start with some specific questions, do you agree with me in general that a human being is in general more capable to recall details of events that took place in recent times than events that occurred a long time ago? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: In fact, you -- I want to start with some questions regarding the arrest of the 12 Serbs. Is it correct to say that you know the 12 Serbs personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I personally knew most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You know where they worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I knew where most of them worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to come back to the first initial statement you have given to the Prosecutor. You mentioned, as my learned colleague Mr. Alarid already mentioned you, you mentioned a Lukic was a member of this group; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: If you're thinking of Sredoje, it's correct that he was in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: In your initial statement you said this Lukic is the brother of the notorious Lukic. Is this your statement in the initial statement that you have given to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not absolutely sure if that is what it says. It's possible. If you have the statement in front of you, then I have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: But you say it was Sredoje Lukic who was a member of this 12?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you know the profession -- and you know the profession of Sredoje Lukic at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And the profession of Sredoje Lukic at this time was that he was an ordinary policeman. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I -- from what I know, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: He was an ordinary policeman in the time before the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: During your testimony you have given in the Vasiljevic case, there comes also a time when you have been asked about the arrest of the 12 Serbs, and is it true to your statement that the arrest -- the first arrest of these 12 happened at the 7, 8, or 9th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I cannot be quite sure about the date right now, but that was in that period and probably that is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And the arrest of these 12 was done by police forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: That's what I was told, that that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Today and during your testimony in the Vasiljevic case, you told that neither of these 12 belonged to the police force or army or any Territorial Defence. This is your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. At the time that they were arrested, they were not officially members of the police force or the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: To your recollection and remembrance, Sredoje Lukic was not a member of the police in the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic was a policeman, I believe. I would see him on the street and so on, until a certain date when he left the police station of -- on his own and then joined these informal armed groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Only sometime later in your statement -- in your testimony in the Vasiljevic procedure, you stated that some of those people who had been taken into custody were members of the regular police force. It is on page 138, lines 16 and 17 of the transcripts in English version. This was your statement in Vasiljevic, that these people who has been in custody, some of them were members of the regular police force.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. And when I said that, what I meant was that they worked in that capacity before they were arrested, but I don't think that at the moment that they were arrested they were members of the police forces, because if you allow, it wouldn't make sense for the police to arrest one of their own members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: That's a good point. May I address you to another point. You have been called to take part in negotiations, as you have already explained. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And that you have been called for negotiations, it was after the arrest of the 12th by the police. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. There were some talks earlier, but in relation to this group, yes, that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Very fine. And at this time you have been called to take part in negotiations, a person, Murat Sabanovic and his men have already occupied the dam at the Drina River. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I think that in that period a little bit before or a little bit after, but anyway, in that area Murat Sabanovic was at the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My question was: In the moment when you started the negotiations, Murat Sabanovic had occupied the dam, still occupied the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I think that he was there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And there was a situation that water was released from this dam. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could it be -- I'm sorry. Could it be the 13th of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible that that is the date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And the first negotiations you have participated in had taken place one day after the water was released. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: I think that we had telephone contacts prior to that as well, but at that particular point in time we had direct contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And the water was released by Murat Sabanovic and his men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way, although they were not trained. They were not capable of actually handling the equipment. There were professionals who were working at the dam, and they did so at their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And in the moment the 12 Serbs has been released, these 12 Serbs has been at the dam. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I'm not sure I quite got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Okay. In the moment the 12 Serbs has been released in the end, in this moment the 12 Serbs has been at the dam? It means they have been released at the dam, in freedom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Yes. The decision to set them free was taken in Medjedja where the municipal echelons were working and managing affairs at the time. They were handed over to the Yugoslav army's soldiers who were at the dam. They were handed over to them at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And the 12 Serbs has been arrested by police and has been transferred to the dam afterwards; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could not say anything about their movement with precision. I did hear a story to the effect that at a certain point in time they were at the dam also, but they moved around. They were at a number of locations when they were arrested, as it were, when they were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So you agree with me that first of all they had been arrested in police detention and in the end they had been at the dam; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-022
utterances.text: Well, as I said, they were at the police station. After that, they changed locations, and I heard that for a while they had also been at the dam feature and ultimately, at the end, they were in the settlement of Medjedja where the police and the municipal organs of authority had also transferred themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
